quick.summary: Why wide tables are slow, and how separating events from entities speeds them up.
quick.takeaway: Split your data into things that happened and things that exist.

beats.line: Our giant sales table takes ten minutes to load. Why is it so slow?
Imagine a cafe receipt. It lists your coffee, but not the recipe.
Right, the recipe lives in a cookbook in the back.
Exactly. If every receipt printed the recipe, paper would run out fast.
Tables work the same way. We separate what happened from what things are.
Data engineers call this dimensional modeling.
Can I just say events and things?
Yes. Events grow every second. Things change slowly.
So I put orders in one table, and store products in another?
Now you are building a fast warehouse.

quiz.question: How do you design tables to keep queries fast?
options: Put everything in one giant table.
Split data into events and things.
Only save events and delete the things.
Make the user download a spreadsheet.
quiz.explanation: Separating fast-growing events from slow-changing things makes tables smaller and much faster to search.

quiz.question: You should repeat a product’s full details on every sales record to save time.
quiz.explanation: That wastes space and goes stale when the product changes. Store the details once, in their own table.
